sections.heading: What is the Hashing & Frequency Map Pattern?
sections.content: Hashing uses a HashMap or HashSet to answer questions like 'have I seen this before?', 'how many times does this appear?' and 'where did I last see it?' in O(1) average time. By trading O(n) extra memory for fast lookups, you replace an inner loop with a single lookup and turn many O(n²) solutions into O(n). It is the most common optimization in DSA and a building block for other patterns such as sliding window and prefix sum.

sections.heading: When to Use It
items: Count how often each element appears (frequency map)
Check for duplicates or membership quickly (HashSet)
Find a pair or complement (Two Sum, 4Sum variants)
Group items that share a property (anagrams, same pattern)
Track the first or last position of a value
Compare two collections for equal contents
Remember previous results (caching, memoization)
Keywords: count, frequency, duplicate, anagram, group, unique, first non-repeating, complement

sections.heading: Hashing Basics in Kotlin
sections.content: A HashMap computes a hash code from the key to find a bucket, so lookups, inserts and deletes are O(1) on average. In the worst case (many collisions) they degrade, but this is rare in practice. Keys must have stable hashCode() and equals(). Strings, numbers, Pairs and data classes work well. Arrays and mutable lists are poor keys because they use identity hashing or change after insertion.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
items: Inserting x into the map before checking for its complement in Two Sum, so x pairs with itself
Using arrays or mutable lists as keys (they compare by reference or can change)
Forgetting that map[key] returns null, then using !! on a missing key
Modifying a map while iterating over it, which throws ConcurrentModificationException
Assuming HashMap keeps insertion order (use LinkedHashMap for that)
Using a HashMap<Char, Int> when a 26-length IntArray is simpler and faster
Ignoring worst-case O(n) behavior with adversarial keys in contests
Counting wrong for duplicates: use counts, not a set, when multiplicity matters

sections.heading: Key Takeaways
items: HashMap and HashSet give O(1) average lookups and replace inner loops
Use a frequency map to count, a set to detect repeats, and a map to remember positions
In Two Sum style problems, check for the complement before inserting the current value
Group by a signature (sorted letters, count array, pattern) to cluster related items
Use IntArray(26) instead of HashMap when keys are lowercase letters
Never use arrays or mutable collections as hash keys; use Pair, String or a data class
